name: Podcast mic and EQ boost

lead: Pairing a close, directional microphone with a low-frequency EQ boost makes a recorded voice sound deeper, warmer and more resonant. The effect is audible straight away on recordings.

Directional microphones such as cardioids boost bass when the source is very close, called the proximity effect, which radio announcers are often said to use for an authoritative tone. EQ is a separate, electronic adjustment of frequency balance that can add more low end.

paras: People speak close to a directional mic and apply a low-end boost in the recording software, often for podcasts, streams and voice messages.
No health risks are documented. The effect exists only in the recording or broadcast, and the speaker's live voice is unchanged.

angle.text: A close directional mic adds bass through the proximity effect, and a low-end EQ boost adds more, so recordings sound deeper, fuller and more resonant. Your own voice stays the same.

lead: A podcast microphone with an equalizer (EQ) boost is a recording setup in which a directional microphone is used close to the mouth and low frequencies are raised electronically, so that a recorded voice sounds deeper or fuller. It is discussed in voice-focused corners of appearance and self-improvement culture as a way to make a recorded voice sound more resonant.

Part of the effect is acoustic. Directional microphones such as cardioids boost bass when the sound source is very close, a phenomenon called the proximity effect, which makes voices sound warmer and fuller and which radio announcers are often said to use for an authoritative tone.[1] Equalization is the separate, electronic adjustment of frequency balance. The change affects only the recording or broadcast, not the speaker's own voice.
infobox: Proximity effect (bass boost at close range)[1]

paras: In directional microphones, sound reaches both sides of the diaphragm, and at very short distances the pressure difference favors low frequencies, tilting the response toward bass. Omnidirectional microphones generally do not show the effect. Engineers who find the boost unwanted may change microphone type or working distance.[1]
